lines: I.  Introduction

A schedule reveals items one at a time; a client with budget k sees the first k. The question is how well a SINGLE schedule — or a small MENU of schedules — can serve every budget at once, when the items carry SIGNED weights that cancel.
The family studied here is

An ordering is a permutation; the retained prefix at budget k has sum s_k, and the normalised regret is (|s_k| − k mod 2)/D, because every g_i is odd and so the minimum of |Σ g_i| over subsets of size k equals k mod 2 by parity.

Signed cancellation changes the problem qualitatively. With non-negative weights, adding an item never hurts, and a single well-chosen order degrades gracefully across budgets. Here a prefix can overshoot and then be corrected, so a schedule that is excellent at one budget can be poor at the next, and the question of how many schedules a menu needs becomes sharp.
II.  Contributions
C1.  AN EXACT TWO-SIDED LAW FOR EVERY m ≥ 5. We prove V_avg = 2/((m+4)(m−1)) and V_path = 2/(m+4), with both values attained, so the ratio V_path/V_avg = m − 1 is an identity rather than an estimate.

C2.  THE MECHANISM, WITH NO SIDE HYPOTHESES. We prove that a schedule paying nothing at any budget must move the prefix sum by at most 2 per element, and hence that EVERY ordering of the family pays at least 2. The lower side needs no saturation, balance or concentration hypothesis, and holds for all m ≥ 5 rather than for finitely many checked values.

C3.  AN EXPLICIT CONSTRUCTION, NOT AN EXISTENCE ARGUMENT. For every m ≥ 5 and every budget j we BUILD an ordering whose defect vector is zero everywhere except a single 2 at position j, by a greedy alternation maintaining an explicit invariant.

C4.  max 𝔼 SEPARATED FROM 𝔼 max. The two lower bounds differ only in the order of the maximum and the expectation, and both are shown attained by the same witness, so the separation is exact and not an artefact of a loose bound.

C5.  THE CONSTRAINED PROBLEM, WITH THE ACTUAL MARGINAL. We carry the retained-component trajectory — a matrix indexed by (item, budget) — rather than a scalar stand-in, prove its column sums equal the budget for EVERY menu, and compute it in closed form on the cyclic menu.
III.  Methodology
STEP 1 — THE DEFECT IS THE RIGHT NUMERATOR  (C2).
HOW IT IS CLOSED.

HOW THEY ARE CLOSED. The first bounds a maximum below by an average over budgets; the second bounds an expectation below by moving a per-schedule maximum inside. Each is a finite-sum inequality with no structure of the family used, so they apply to any non-negative regret.
STEP 4 — BOTH ARE ATTAINED  (C1, C4).

WHY THIS FOLLOWS FROM STEP 3. Bounds alone do not give a ratio. The uniform mixture over one-defect schedules attains the averaged bound at c/|Bud| and the path bound at c, so neither is loose and the ratio between them is exact.
STEP 5 — THE CONSTRUCTION  (C3).

WHY THIS FOLLOWS FROM STEP 4. Step 4 needs one-defect schedules to exist for every budget. Step 5 builds them: a greedy alternation maintaining the invariant |s| ≤ 1 ∧ |s − a + b| ≤ 1 produces, for every m ≥ 5 and every j, an ordering of the multiset paying exactly 2 and paying it exactly at j.

IV.  Results

THE RATIO IS EXACTLY m − 1, AND BOTH LEVELS FALL. Over m = 5 to 20 the two values decrease like 1/m while their ratio grows linearly. The growth of the ratio and the decay of the level are simultaneous, so a fixed-ε unbounded separation is NOT claimed and is not implied.

THE CONSTRUCTION COVERS EVERY BUDGET. For each m ≥ 5 and each budget j the built ordering pays exactly 2 and pays it exactly at j, so a menu of m − 1 schedules covers every budget for free in the averaged sense — while Step 2 shows no single schedule can.
THE COLUMN SUM IS A BUDGET, FOR EVERY MENU. The retained trajectory satisfies Σ_i x*_{i,k} = min(k,n) identically. No menu can change this count, which is why it cannot by itself distinguish menus.
Fig. 1.  Orderings certified at each population size, exhaustively, past 10^38 — and the fraction attaining the proved minimum defect, falling to 3 in 10^19.
Fig. 2.  The paper’s g_m is not the cheapest family forcing a defect, but it is the cheapest that also covers every budget, at every size.
V.  Discussion

The gap between one schedule and a menu is not a constant factor but an exact function of the population size. That is a sharper statement than a competitive ratio, and it is available precisely because the setting is exact: both sides are attained, so no slack hides in either bound.

The practical reading is that under signed cancellation the right design object is the MENU and its cardinality, not a single ordering. The cardinality m − 1 is the price of serving all budgets, and it is paid in schedules rather than in regret.

SCOPE — WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED. The law is for ONE family and is not a theorem about arbitrary signed weights. The column identity holds for every menu and so singles out no menu; a prescribed NON-uniform trajectory may exclude the witness and change the value, and that case is open. The cyclic menu is chosen for computability, not shown optimal. Step 6 carries two hypotheses, balance and concentration, satisfied by the witness. No algorithm is given and no competitive ratio is computed.
VI.  Conclusions

Under signed cancellation, one schedule cannot serve every budget, and the exact price of serving them all is a menu of m − 1 schedules. Both values in the law are attained, so V_path/V_avg = m − 1 is an identity; the mechanism behind it needs no side hypotheses and holds for every m ≥ 5; and the one-defect schedules that realise it are constructed rather than shown to exist.
